p.title: Measuring stance dynamics in political debate using temporal graph neural networks

ext.title: Measuring stance dynamics in political debate using temporal graph neural networks
ext.venue: Information Processing and Management, vol. 63, article 104705 (published online 4 March 2026; open access, CC BY). Metadata hint corrected: full author names, volume and article number, and DOI taken from the text.
ext.document_type: Journal article (empirical ML / computational social science, Twitter stance inference)
ext.coverage: Full text read in three chunks covering all 1,134 lines of the extracted text (lines 0-399, 400-849, 850-1133), including abstract, introduction, related work, methods (Sec. 3, Eqs. 1-12, Algorithm 1), experiments (Sec. 4), stance-shift analysis (Sec. 5), discussion, limitations (Sec. 6.1), CRediT and data statements, and the full reference list. Paul's markup: no markup files were supplied (the task listed none), so paul_markup is empty. Not in the text file: supplementary material (Figs. S1-S2, Tables S1-S4), so the 5-fold CV table, the baseline gap in Fig. 2, and the per-period counts are not available here. Figures 2, 4, 5 and 6 are described only in the text, so their plotted values are not extracted. Page locations use the journal page footers. Relevance check: no lobbying, path-finding, allocation or legislator-level content; elections appear only as the referendum context; networks appear as user-hashtag and user-user graphs; text measurement appears as hashtag-based stance labels and FastText embeddings. Those topics are covered only as they bear on stance measurement.
ext.research_question: Can a temporal graph neural network infer user-level stance (favor vs. against) toward a referendum from user-hashtag and user-user interaction graphs at each 28-day period, including users who never post about the target, and can the resulting trajectories characterize opinion shifts at population, individual and neighborhood levels? (Sec. 1.1, p.2-3.)
ext.theory: Opinion change is treated as incremental, path-dependent and embedded in social context rather than abrupt reversal (Sec. 6, p.16). The model is motivated by social-influence and network-evolution theory (Flache et al., 2017; Bianchi & Squazzoni, 2015) and by the claim that inactive "silent" users keep stance information through embedding persistence across snapshots (Sec. 2 and 6). Social influence and homophily in temporal movement are asserted in the discussion (p.15-16) but are not tested beyond descriptive correlations. No formal opinion-dynamics model is estimated.
ext.data: Two Twitter (now X) datasets on the Chilean constitutional referendums, drawn from users following 384 Chilean news outlets, self-reported in Santiago, with at least 10 tweets across topics (Sec. 3.2, p.4-5). Original pool of about 9.2M users. Entry_DS (referendum of 25 Oct 2020): period 1 Jan to 24 Oct 2020; 849,171 tweets; 12,237 users; 171,615 hashtags; 80 labeled referendum hashtags (23 support, 57 oppose) used by 5,540 users; 11 periods of 28 days. Exit_DS (referendum of 4 Sep 2022): period 1 Jan to 3 Sep 2022; 356,214 tweets; 4,934 users; 57,211 hashtags; 106 labeled hashtags (50 support, 56 oppose) used by 1,897 users; 9 periods of 28 days (Table 1, p.5; Sec. 3.4, p.6). Unit of analysis: user-period snapshot (user stance per 28-day window). Totals across both datasets: about 1.21M tweets and 17,171 user rows (not deduplicated). Ground-truth stance comes from labeled-hashtag interaction counts (Eqs. 1-2). More than 95% of users interact with hashtags from one side only (p.6). Human validation: 100 user snapshots per dataset, two annotators (p.6-7). Word embeddings: FastText CBOW trained on all user-generated content, with preprocessing (Sec. 3.2). Data availability: "on request" (p.17).
ext.method: TWLGCN (Temporal Weighted LightGCN), an extension of WLGCN (Zhou & Elejalde, 2024). Each 28-day snapshot is a bipartite user-hashtag graph with count-weighted edges (Sec. 3.3). Four GCN propagation layers with symmetric degree normalization (Eq. 3), then multi-head attention over layer outputs (Eq. 4). User embeddings go to an MLP classifier with batch norm and dropout. Loss = focal loss (Eq. 5-6, class imbalance) + lambda1 * SSCL + lambda2 * ||H0||^2 (Eq. 11), with lambda1 = 1e-3 and lambda2 = 1e-6 (Sec. 4.1). SSCL, the Supervised Stance Contrastive Loss (Eq. 9-10), treats same-stance users and hashtags as positives and uses the adaptive reweighting alpha(x) = (rho + x)^(-lambda) from DynaDeno (Eq. 8). Noise-based augmentation of embeddings (Eq. 7). Sequential warm start: Xavier initialization at t=0; later periods inherit embeddings and MLP weights; hashtag initial embeddings from period-specific FastText (Sec. 3.3). User-user graphs: Pas (static follower/friend edges) and Act (per-period directed mention/quote/reply edges, Sec. 3.6, Eq. 12). Adam optimizer; max 1000 epochs; early stop after 50 epochs without validation macro-F1 gain. Stance probabilities from hashtag counts: p+ = |R+| / (|R+| + |R-|) (Eq. 1); ties are assigned by larger count, and ambiguous users are kept in training (p.6).
ext.identification: Not a causal design. Leakage control: 5-fold CV on annotated users (80% train / 20% validation). For every validation user, all edges to referendum-labeled hashtags are removed before training and inference, so validation users are "referendum-silent" (Sec. 4.1, p.9). Macro-F1 is computed per period on that period's active validation users. Shift analysis (flip categories, t-SNE distances, neighbor-dynamics heatmaps) is descriptive. Neighbor correlations are described as "potential social influences" (p.14) but no identification strategy is applied. Validation of labels: Cohen's kappa for human vs. human and human vs. hashtag labels (p.7). Open concern (not addressed in the text): FastText embeddings are trained on all user-generated content (Sec. 3.2), which may include validation users' text, and the paper does not say whether that text was restricted to training users.
ext.scope: Population: Twitter/X users in Santiago, Chile, who follow Chilean news outlets and meet activity filters (not representative; the authors say Twitter leaned liberal and supportive of the process, p.12). Institution: the two national constitutional referendums (2020 entry, 2022 exit). Era: January 2020 to September 2022, in 28-day periods. Language: Spanish hashtags (cultural use noted as a generalizability concern, p.16). Scope limited to a single platform and two referendums; no other elections, legislators, lobbying or policy venues.

key_findings.finding: TWLGCN variants keep macro-F1 steady across periods, while the non-TWLGCN baselines (WLGCN, EvolveGCN, DynaDeno) fluctuate much more sharply.
key_findings.numbers: Steady 70%-90% macro-F1 over observed periods; exact baseline values are in Fig. 2 and Table S4 (supplement, not in text).

key_findings.finding: The abstract claims the model beats network-based baselines in macro-F1 by more than 5% at each period using only 0.2% labeled hashtags. The main text does not report the baseline gap numerically, so the claim cannot be checked from the text.
key_findings.numbers: Claimed >5%; labeled hashtags 80/171,615 (about 0.05%) in Entry_DS and 106/57,211 (about 0.19%) in Exit_DS (Table 1, p.5).

key_findings.finding: Carrying embeddings forward across snapshots matters: the full model beats the discrete variant that re-initializes embeddings each period.
key_findings.numbers: On Exit_DS, the full TWLGCN outperforms the discrete variant by 1.3% to 9.8%.

key_findings.finding: Adding active user-user relations (mentions, quotes, replies) gives the best overall performance. Passive follower/friend relations add little, and combining both does not help.
key_findings.numbers: Act improves the base model by about 3% on both datasets.

key_findings.finding: The supervised contrastive loss (SSCL) adds accuracy on top of focal loss. The authors attribute this to same-class contrastive signal.
key_findings.numbers: TWLGCN vs. TWLGCN w/o SSCL: about 2% gain in macro-F1.

key_findings.finding: Human annotators agree substantially with each other on the stance of user snapshots, and with hashtag-derived labels, which supports hashtags as a stance proxy.
key_findings.numbers: Human-human Cohen's kappa 0.836 (Entry_DS) and 0.842 (Exit_DS); human vs. hashtag-derived kappa 0.81 to 0.94; 100 user snapshots per dataset.

key_findings.finding: Population-level stance: the Entry_DS median stays slightly positive (about 0.2) with a small IQR. The Exit_DS median starts below zero and drifts toward positive values, with a widening spread near the referendum date.
key_findings.numbers: Entry_DS median about 0.2; opposing views about 25% of users; Exit_DS median initially negative (no exact value given).

key_findings.finding: Sudden flips between opposing and supporting: the number of O-to-S and S-to-O flips mirror each other across periods, with a sharp rise in supporter-to-opponent flips between periods 7 and 8 in Entry_DS.
key_findings.numbers: No exact counts given in text.

key_findings.finding: Flipping users move in the expected direction in embedding space relative to the annotated-hashtag centroids (periods 10 and 11, Entry_DS).
key_findings.numbers: O-to-S users increase average distance from the opposing-hashtag centroid by over 28%. S-to-O users reduce distance to the opposing centroid by over 10% and increase distance to the supporting centroid by 27%.

key_findings.finding: Neighbors' stance shifts are correlated: users tend to shift in the same direction as their 1-hop and 2-hop neighbors (diagonal dominance). Authors describe this as tight-knit communities moving together; it is a descriptive correlation, not a tested influence effect.
key_findings.numbers: Heatmap values only in figure; no numeric summary in text.

key_findings.finding: Coverage of users present from the first snapshot (users remain predictable in later snapshots even with no activity).
Filtering did not distort the temporal or activity distribution of tweets relative to the raw data.
key_findings.numbers: Cosine similarity > 0.99 and Jensen-Shannon distance < 0.05 for both datasets.

key_findings.finding: Ambiguous users (interacting with both sides) are kept in training because they sit on the semantic boundary.
key_findings.numbers: More than 95% of users interact with one side only.

key_findings.finding: Window length: 28-day windows are chosen by a sensitivity analysis. Shorter windows fragment the graph (low giant-component fraction); longer windows mask rapid polarity shifts.

measures: Macro-F1 per period on contemporaneous validation users (primary metric; chosen over accuracy because of class imbalance)
Stance probability per user per period (MLP output, described as in [-1, 1]); the mapping from MLP probability to that scale is not defined in the text
Stance shift delta p between consecutive periods, classified into seven dynamics (static via med + MAD threshold; O->MO, O->LO, O->S, S->O, S->LS, S->MS) (Sec. 5.2, p.13)
Hashtag-derived stance probabilities from interaction counts p+ = |R+|/(|R+|+|R-|) (Eq. 1)
Cosine similarity between user and hashtag embeddings; top-100 nearest hashtags per user and per annotated hashtag (Sec. 4.3.2)
Centroid distances in embedding space, visualized with t-SNE (100-dimensional representations)
Cohen's kappa for human-human and human-hashtag agreement
Jensen-Shannon distance and cosine similarity for filtering-bias check
limitations: Supervision is narrow: stance labels come only from a small set of referendum hashtags (80 and 106 labeled), so users who avoid those hashtags can only partly be validated (Sec. 6.1, p.16).
Labels are hashtag-derived proxies, with human agreement checked on only 100 snapshots per dataset (Sec. 3.4, p.6-7).

Generalizability: one platform (Twitter/X), two Chilean referendums, Spanish hashtags with cultural use; replication across platforms, elections and languages is needed. Hashtag hijacking is not systematically evaluated (p.16).
Fixed 28-day windows: shorter windows are sparse, longer ones over-smooth event-driven shifts; adaptive windows or continuous-time TGNNs are left for future work (p.16).
Sequential warm-start training (DTDG, online) rather than joint end-to-end temporal optimization, which the authors call a trade-off in favor of streaming use (p.17).
Sample is not representative: Santiago self-reported users following Chilean news outlets; Twitter leaned liberal and mostly supportive of the process (p.12).
Vote outcomes are compared only qualitatively (the entry vote passed, the exit vote did not); no quantitative validation against the vote or polls (p.12).
Neighbor-correlation and 'influence' claims are descriptive; the authors say leaders of shifts are future work (p.15).
Main-text performance gap versus baselines is not given numerically; full CV results are in the supplement (Table S4), not in the extracted text.
Data available only on request (p.17). Multimodal inputs, multitask learning and LLM-based user-level stance are unexplored (p.17).

short_quotes.quote: stance change is typically incremental, path-dependent, and embedded within social contexts

rel.summary_md:
Zhou and Elejalde build TWLGCN, a temporal graph network that infers whether a Twitter user favours or opposes a referendum. It works on a user-hashtag graph rebuilt every 28 days, plus optional user-user edges. The model is trained on only 80 to 106 hashtags labelled by side, from Chile's 2020 and 2022 referendums (about 1.21M tweets; 12,237 and 4,934 users). Each period's embeddings carry into the next. This beats re-starting each period by 1.3% to 9.8% on the 2022 dataset. Mention, quote and reply edges add about 3% macro-F1; follower edges add little. Labels taken from hashtags agree with human coders (kappa 0.81 to 0.94, on 100 snapshots per dataset). The second half is descriptive: seven classes of movement per transition, with a "static" band of median + MAD; flip curves that mirror each other; and neighbours who tend to shift in the same direction (Fig. 6). There is no null baseline and no causal test.

This matters because `fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py` is an explicit port of this paper, without the GNN. It uses 91-day windows on the CU press corpus, carries a member's last stance through silent windows, uses the seven-dynamics taxonomy, tests whether neighbours move together, and proposes stances for silent members from their neighbours. Checked against the live output (`data/stance/stance_dynamics.json`), the port has three problems. The paper's static band assumes a continuous probability. On pooled stance signs it comes out at 0.708, so almost every move counts as static. The neighbour co-movement test is null (134 same / 122 opposite, 52%). The 77.5% sign agreement for imputation (n=1,087) has no party or majority-class baseline, while the paper scores with macro-F1 because its classes are imbalanced. The paper backs the design ideas. It does not validate carrying a label forward, the 91-day window, or the imputation. All of those remain UNVERIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: Stance is a trajectory over discrete 28-day snapshots. Embeddings persist so that silent users keep a stance. Transitions fall into seven dynamics with a static band of median + MAD (O->MO, O->LO, O->S, S->O, S->LS, S->MS). Mirror-image O->S / S->O flip curves flag external events. Users with no stance are inferred from neighbours.
bearings.system_side: The module docstring says it transplants all five ideas without the GNN. It uses 13-week windows over the CU press corpus, carries the last stance, uses the seven-dynamics taxonomy, builds flip curves, tests neighbour co-movement, and writes silent-member imputation proposals to a CSV without touching the matrix.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The design vocabulary carries over. The paper's evidence does not: its numbers come from a trained GNN on about 1.2M Spanish tweets from ordinary users, while the system pools 2.4k press items from members of Congress by quarter. None of the paper's performance figures transfer to this module.

bearings.paper_claim: The static band (|delta p| <= median + MAD) is applied to continuous stance probabilities from an MLP for users who post in nearly every 28-day period.
bearings.system_side: The band is computed from observed-to-observed transitions of a confidence-weighted mean of stance_sign in {-1,0,+1}, with a floor of 0.05. In the live output the band is 0.7076 on a [-1,1] scale, so any move smaller than about 0.71 counts as static. Only near-sign reversals register as movement, which empties the O->LO, S->LS and similar classes by construction.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The band only means what the paper intends when stance is continuous and densely observed. With signs pooled over sparse quarterly press, median + MAD measures how discrete the labels are, not how much a member's stance moved. The paper gives no support for the seven-class counts the system produces.

bearings.paper_claim: Users tend to shift in the same direction as their 1-hop and 2-hop neighbours (diagonal dominance in Fig. 6). This is described as tight-knit communities moving together; the authors present it as a descriptive correlation with no null model and no identification.
bearings.system_side: Co-movement is counted as same versus opposite direction among neighbours who both move in a window, with an ad hoc threshold of 0.55 for 'diagonal dominance'. Live result on cosponsor ties: same 134 / opposite 122 (52%), null; the brain records HCoI at 49%, also null. There is no permutation baseline and no control for common shocks within a window.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's positive result comes from a communication graph of ordinary Twitter users at 28-day resolution. The system tests cosponsorship and press-topic layers at quarterly resolution. Neither result has a null. A common shock in one window would raise 'same' counts in both settings, so the paper's finding cannot overturn the system's null, and the null cannot refute the paper. Influence language is not warranted on either side.

bearings.paper_claim: Inference for silent users is validated by 5-fold CV. Each validation user's edges to labelled hashtags are removed before training ('referendum-silent'). Results are scored by macro-F1 per period, chosen over accuracy because of class imbalance (steady 70%-90%).
bearings.system_side: Imputation takes the mean tier score of at least 5 cosponsor neighbours and keeps proposals where |est| >= 0.75. The 'masking validation' reports raw sign agreement against the member's known label: 77.5% on n=1,087 cells, with 307 proposals. No party-only or majority-class baseline is reported. True Neutral counts as a negative sign. The final print says '>=3 informative neighbors' while MINNB is 5.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Cosponsor neighbours are mostly co-partisan, and the stance matrix has known party confounds (the CFPB tiers). A 77.5% sign agreement may therefore be no better than a party or majority baseline. The paper's protocol implies the system should report macro-F1 or a party baseline before treating the 77.5% as signal. That figure stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until a second path reproduces it.

bearings.paper_claim: Carrying learned embeddings and MLP weights forward between snapshots beats re-initialising each period by 1.3% to 9.8% (Exit_DS). The 28-day window was chosen by a sensitivity analysis on the giant-component fraction: shorter windows fragment the graph and longer ones mask rapid shifts.
bearings.system_side: 'Persistence' copies the last observed raw stance into silent windows. Carried windows also enter the transition counts (so static counts are inflated, and a flip across a silent gap is credited to the window where posting resumes). The 91-day window is set by assertion in a comment, with no sensitivity run.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's gain from persistence comes from warm-starting a learned representation that keeps updating from new edges. It does not support freezing a label. The window rule (largest-component fraction against shift masking) can be ported, but it needs a graph rebuilt per window, which the press corpus does not supply.

bearings.paper_claim: Active user-user relations per period (mentions, quotes, replies) give the best stance inference, about +3% macro-F1 on both datasets. Passive follower/friend edges add little, and combining the two does not help.
bearings.system_side: The system already builds a directed member-member interaction layer (reposts w 1.0, mentions w 0.4, author-volume normalised, pair cap 0.25). It feeds the multilayer cascade network. stance_dynamics tests co-movement and imputes stances only on the cosponsor and HCoI layers, never on this interaction layer.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's evidence is that interaction edges help stance inference, not that they carry influence. Members' accounts are run by staff and post far less than the paper's users, so expect sparser edges. Any test belongs in the descriptive or proposal lane. This does not license reading the layer as influence or closeness.

gaps_exposed: No null or permutation baseline for neighbour co-movement (for example, shuffled neighbours within a window, or a control for common shocks per window). The 0.55 'diagonal dominance' threshold is arbitrary (stance_dynamics.py:106).

The imputation is scored by raw sign agreement (77.5%, n=1,087). There is no macro-F1 and no party-only or majority-class baseline, even though the component's own open question asks for a party baseline.
The static band is unusable on pooled sign data: it is 0.7076 live, so the seven-dynamics classes other than flips are nearly empty by construction.
The 91-day window has no sensitivity analysis. The paper picks its window from giant-component fraction against shift masking.
Carried (silent) windows enter the transition counts, inflating static counts and moving flips to the window where posting resumes.
Co-movement and imputation are never run on the repost/mention interaction layer, which is the analog of the paper's best-performing Act edges.
Documentation drift: the print at stance_dynamics.py:152 says '>=3 informative neighbors' while MINNB defaults to 5.
flags: The neighbour co-movement result (in the paper's Fig. 6, and in any re-run here) is a descriptive correlation. It must not be described as influence or contagion, and the paper's 'potential social influences' wording should not be carried into system text.

The paper's symmetric degree normalisation inside GCN propagation (Eq. 3) is message-passing normalisation, not an argument for per-edge volume normalisation of SNA edges. That proposal was measured and REJECTED in this project, so it must not be cited as support for reviving it.
The 77.5% imputation sign agreement and the 52% / 49% co-movement nulls are single-path agent analyses: UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until a second path reproduces them.
Imputed stances remain proposals only. Stance labels are Paul's domain, and the module correctly leaves the matrix untouched.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's annotation is a bare link ('Neural Networks link, sciencedirect S0306457326000968') with no takeaways. His component position lists the paper as a 'possible Neural Networks link' under stance-dynamics and says he wants temporal dynamics and modelling of how likely stances are to change. That note is stale. The link is not just possible: stance_dynamics.py has been an explicit port of this paper since the July 2026 enhancement wave, and the port's co-movement test came back null (52% cosponsor, 49% HCoI), which his notes predate. The paper partly agrees with what he wants: it supports treating stance as a trajectory and inferring stances for silent actors. But it gives no change-likelihood model; its shift analysis is descriptive. Its gains come from a trained GNN on dense tweet data, which the system deliberately did not build. Read correctly, the paper calls for better validation of the existing port (baselines, a working static band, a window sensitivity run), not more machinery.

related.why: Its HCoI communities form the second layer on which stance_dynamics.py tests this paper's neighbour co-movement claim (null, 49%).
It arrived in the same July 2026 enhancement wave and covers the Twitter-data measurement issues behind this paper's hashtag-proxy labels and interaction edges.
Both infer stance from political tweets. Khan compares text classifiers on single tweets; this paper infers user-level stance from the graph with minimal text supervision.
An alternative route to stance detection (LLM plus logic tensor network) next to this paper's graph-propagation route. The authors list LLM-based user stance as future work.
Explains the sampling-bias limits this paper concedes: a liberal-leaning Santiago Twitter sample of news-outlet followers.
Both use graph neural network embeddings on social graphs, Kumar for seed selection and this paper for stance inference.
